english.ad_engine_db_605_4x_desc: Bored-out development of the DB 601 with roughly 42,400 built, hindered by bearing and lubricant reliability issues. Four-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_db_606_2x_desc: Twin coupled DB 601 engines driving a single reduction gearbox, weighing around 1.5 tonnes and notorious for in-flight engine fires due to inadequate nacelle cooling. Twin-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_db_606_4x_desc: Twin coupled DB 601 engines driving a single reduction gearbox, weighing around 1.5 tonnes and notorious for in-flight engine fires due to inadequate nacelle cooling. Four-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_db_610_2x_desc: Twin coupled DB 605 powerplant serving as the heart of Germany's only operational heavy bomber. Twin-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_db_610_4x_desc: Twin coupled DB 605 powerplant serving as the heart of Germany's only operational heavy bomber. Four-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_jumo_205_2x_desc: Junkers opposed-piston two-stroke diesel engine with about 900 built; economical for long-range maritime patrol despite sluggish throttle response. Twin-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_jumo_205_4x_desc: Junkers opposed-piston two-stroke diesel engine with about 900 built; economical for long-range maritime patrol despite sluggish throttle response. Four-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_jumo_207_2x_desc: High-altitude turbocharged and intercooled derivative of the Jumo 205 (200–300 built), enabling reconnaissance flights above 12 km. Twin-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_jumo_207_4x_desc: High-altitude turbocharged and intercooled derivative of the Jumo 205 (200–300 built), enabling reconnaissance flights above 12 km. Four-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_jumo_210_2x_desc: Germany's first mass-produced inverted V12 gasoline aircraft engine. Twin-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_jumo_210_4x_desc: Germany's first mass-produced inverted V12 gasoline aircraft engine. Four-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_jumo_211_2x_desc: Germany's highest-production aircraft engine of the war, with 68,248 units built. Twin-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_jumo_211_4x_desc: Germany's highest-production aircraft engine of the war, with 68,248 units built. Four-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_jumo_213_2x_desc: Pressurized-cooling, high-RPM development of the Jumo 211 sharing mounting points with the DB 603. Twin-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_jumo_213_4x_desc: Pressurized-cooling, high-RPM development of the Jumo 211 sharing mounting points with the DB 603. Four-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_jumo_004_2x_desc: The world's first mass-produced axial-flow turbojet with around 8,000 built. Due to nickel and chromium shortages, the 004B used steel turbine blades with an overhaul life of roughly 25 hours. Twin-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_jumo_004_4x_desc: The world's first mass-produced axial-flow turbojet with around 8,000 built. Due to nickel and chromium shortages, the 004B used steel turbine blades with an overhaul life of roughly 25 hours. Four-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_bmw_003_2x_desc: Germany's second mass-produced turbojet with around 3,500 built; lower thrust than the Jumo 004, but smaller in diameter and more fuel-efficient. Twin-engine installation.
english.ad_engine_bmw_003_4x_desc: Germany's second mass-produced turbojet with around 3,500 built; lower thrust than the Jumo 004, but smaller in diameter and more fuel-efficient. Four-engine installation.
english.ad_bomb_fritzx_1x_desc: Fritz X (PC 1400 X) radio-guided armor-piercing glide bomb, weighing approximately 1,570 kg (including a 320 kg warhead).
english.ad_baymine_lm_a_desc: LM A air-dropped naval ground mine, weighing approximately 500 kg.
english.ad_baymine_lm_b_desc: LM B air-dropped naval ground mine, weighing approximately 1,000 kg.
english.ad_baymine_lmb_iii_desc: LMB III air-dropped naval mine, weighing approximately 1,000 kg.
english.ad_torpedo_ltf5a_1x_desc: LT F5a aerial torpedo, weighing approximately 685 kg.
english.ad_torpedo_ltf5a_2x_desc: LT F5a aerial torpedo, weighing approximately 685 kg.
english.ad_torpedo_ltf5b_1x_desc: LT F5b aerial torpedo, weighing approximately 765 kg (448 mm caliber, 200 kg warhead).
english.ad_torpedo_ltf5b_2x_desc: LT F5b aerial torpedo, weighing approximately 765 kg (448 mm caliber, 200 kg warhead).
english.ad_torpedo_ltf5w_1x_desc: LT F5w aerial torpedo (Italian Fiume production), weighing approximately 750 kg.
english.ad_torpedo_ltf5w_2x_desc: LT F5w aerial torpedo (Italian Fiume production), weighing approximately 750 kg.
english.ad_droptank_150l_desc: 150 L jettisonable drop tank, empty weight approximately 18 kg.
english.ad_droptank_300l_desc: 300 L jettisonable drop tank, empty weight approximately 27 kg.
english.ad_droptank_900l_desc: 900 L jettisonable drop tank, empty weight approximately 50 kg.
english.ad_recon_camera_desc: A set of cameras with special lenses that allow aircraft to take precise photographs of enemy formations and installations from high altitude.
english.ad_mg131_4x_desc: 13×64mm B heavy aircraft machine gun capable of firing high-explosive and incendiary ammunition.
english.ad_mg15115_1x_desc: 15×96mm heavy aircraft machine gun with high muzzle velocity and strong armor penetration.
english.ad_mg17_1x_desc: 7.92×57mm belt-fed closed-bolt aircraft machine gun suitable for synchronized firing through the propeller arc.
english.ad_mg17_3x_desc: 7.92×57mm belt-fed closed-bolt aircraft machine gun suitable for synchronized firing through the propeller arc.
english.ad_mg17_4x_desc: 7.92×57mm belt-fed closed-bolt aircraft machine gun suitable for synchronized firing through the propeller arc.
english.ad_mg81_1x_desc: 7.92×57mm belt-fed single-barrel machine gun developed for high rates of fire in aircraft installations.
english.ad_cannon_bk_37_2x_desc: 37×263mm B heavy anti-tank aircraft cannon carried in underwing gun pods.
english.ad_cannon_mg_151_20_2x_desc: Belt-fed 20×82mm aircraft cannon serving as the primary Luftwaffe fighter armament.
english.ad_cannon_mg_151_20_4x_desc: Belt-fed 20×82mm aircraft cannon serving as the primary Luftwaffe fighter armament.
english.ad_cannon_mg_ff_2x_desc: Early drum-fed 20×80mm RB aircraft cannon fitted in the wings of single-engine fighters and the noses of twin-engine destroyers.
english.ad_cannon_mg_ff_m_2x_desc: Improved MG FF modified to fire thin-walled Minengeschoss high-explosive shells.
english.ad_cannon_mk_103_2x_desc: Improved belt-fed 30×184mm B heavy cannon suitable for both motor-cannon and gun-pod installations.
english.ad_cannon_mk_108_2x_desc: Compact 30×90mm RB autocannon firing heavy high-explosive shells, standard armament on late-war interceptors, night fighters, and jets.
english.ad_cannon_mk_108_4x_desc: Compact 30×90mm RB autocannon firing heavy high-explosive shells, standard armament on late-war interceptors, night fighters, and jets.
english.ad_bomb_fritzx_3x_desc: Fritz X (PC 1400 X) radio-guided armor-piercing glide bomb, weighing approximately 1,570 kg (including a 320 kg warhead).
english.ad_droptank_900l_2x_desc: Pair of 900 L jettisonable drop tanks, combined empty weight approximately 100 kg.
english.ad_defense_mk_108_desc: 30×90mm RB MK 108 cannon in upward-firing Schräge Musik dorsal installations.
english.ad_defense_mg_ff_m_desc: 20×80mm RB MG FF/M cannon firing Minengeschoss high-explosive shells in upward-firing Schräge Musik dorsal installations.
english.ad_air_component_folder_desc: Technologies related to aircraft components and air force systems.
english.ad_me_109_fighter_equipment_1_desc: In 1933, the Reich Air Ministry finished a study which called for a fighter to have a top speed of 400 km/h at 6,000m and to be armed with a single 20mm MGC/30 or two 7.92mm MG 17s or one lightweight 20mm MG FF cannon with two MG 17s. The BF 109 was Willy Messerschmitt’s design proposal. When it debuted, the BF109 set speed records, though its armament was lacking when compared to rival aircraft in production in England. Compared to the BF109A, the B added an engine-mounted machine gun. Due to overheating and engine vibrations, the third machine gun was unreliable.
english.ad_me_109_fighter_equipment_2_desc: The BF109C saw strengthened wings which allowed for an additional two MG17s, bringing total armament to four. In addition, a more powerful engine, the Jumo 210G with direct fuel injection was installed.\nObsolete BF109Bs can be converted to BF109Cs.
english.ad_me_109_early_fighter_equipment_1_desc: Produced in 1938, the Bf 109 D had an increased armament of four machine guns. It was intended to showcase the DB-600 engine, but the DB-600 was considered a failure and the Bf 109 would have to wait for the DB-601.
english.ad_me_109_mid_fighter_equipment_1_desc: With the new DB 601A engine more widely available, the Bf 109 E was installed with the new powerplant, which greatly increased the plane’s performance. To accompany the longer and larger engine, there was a major redesign of the airframe to help cool the engine.  A few variants of the Bf 109 Es became the first operational Jagdbomber or fighter bomber with an ETC 500 bomb rack, carrying one 250kg bomb or four 50kg bombs.\n\nDue to major changes, obsolete Bf 109s cannot be converted to Bf 109 Es.
english.ad_me_109_late_fighter_equipment_1_desc: An improved engine, the DB 601E, along with a new wing design and more aerodynamically friendly cooling design greatly increased the performance, speed, and fuel efficiency of the aircraft. Armed with two 7.92 MG 17s and a new Motorkanone cannon firing through the propeller, the plane’s armament was less than the Bf 109 E but had better speed and overall performance.\n\nObsolete BF109Es can be converted to BF109Fs.
english.ad_me_109_late_fighter_equipment_2_desc: To address pilot’s concern about the lack of firepower, the Motorkanone was replaced with new 20mm Mauser MG 151/20 with 200 rounds. Additional improvements to the engine and propeller gave the plane better speed and performance at higher altitudes.\n\nObsolete BF109Fs can be converted to BF109F-4s.
english.ad_me_109_late_fighter_equipment_3_desc: The Bf 109 G series used identical airframes compared to the F series, though the wings were strengthened, a better bullet-proof windshield, and light-alloy armor for the fuel tanks were added. A new and improved DB 605A engine was installed, however there were teething problems which effected the efficiency of the plane. Early versions of the G series carried the same armament as the F series, but G-5 onwards the 7.92mm MG17s were replaced with 13mm MG131s, in addition to a 30mm MK 108 cannon.\n\nDue to major changes, obsolete Bf 109Fs cannot be converted to Bf 109Gs.
english.ad_me_109_late_fighter_equipment_4_desc: The Bf 109 G-14 was an attempt to standardize the production of the G series and incorporated many of the previous features like the DB 605A engine, the improved armament, better cockpit and improved communication. The attempt at standardization failed but did not affect combat performance.\n\nObsolete BF109Gs can be converted to BF109G-14s.
english.ad_me_109_late_fighter_equipment_5_desc: The Bf 109 K was a response to the staggering array of series, models, modification kits, and factory conversions of the Bf 109. The goal behind the design was to create a standard model with more interchangeable parts, equipment, and fix flaws in the design of the airframe. The aircraft used a new engine the DB 605 DB/DC engine which had an injection system which increased the speed of the plane. Planned variants would have increased the armament by adding an additional two 13mm MG131 above the engine, otherwise the plane was armed with two 13mm MG131s and one 30mm MK 108 cannon.\n\nObsolete BF109G-14s can be converted to BF109Ks.
english.ad_me_109_t_fighter_equipment_1_desc: With the Graf Zeppelin under construction, the need for a modern fighter that was carrier-capable was paramount. Testing on the land variants of the Bf 109 B, C, D and E had shown the aircraft’s wings need to be enlarged, the need for a tail-hook, and catapult fittings. The design work lead to the creation of the Bf 109 T, with the T-2 variant being similar in capabilities to the Bf 109 E. However, when the Graf Zeppelin was cancelled, interest in the Bf 109 T subsided and existing planes were stationed in Norway, which suited the plane’s ability to take off and land on short runways.
english.ad_bf_109_h_equipment_1_desc: The Bf 109 H was intended to be a high-altitude fighter based off the F-series. The wingspan was increased, and a stabilizer was added to the fuselage. Several variants were built using the DB 601E and DB 605A engines. Due to issues with wing flutter problems, the plane was scrapped and never entered full production.
english.ad_bf_109_z_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Bf 109 Z was an experimental aircraft which joined two Bf 109F airframes together, similar to the F-82 Twin Mustang. Several variants were proposed, an interceptor armed with five 30mm cannons MK 108 cannons, a fighter-bomber with two 30mm cannons and up two 1,000kg bombs. Only one Bf 109 Z was built and never left the planet’s surface as it was damaged in its hangar by a bombing raid. The project was abandoned shortly afterwards.
english.ad_bf_110_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Reich Air Ministry was looking for multipurpose fighter with a long range, internal bomb bay that was three-seat, twin-engine, and was armed with a cannon. Willy Messerschmitt responded with a design that omitted the bomb bay and increased the planes armament. The Bf110 outperformed rivals Focke-Wulf and Henschel.  The first model, the Bf 110 A was underpowered with DB 600 engines and armed with only four 7.92 MG 17s. The Bf 110 B carried the same engine but was armed with four MG17s and two 20mm MG FF cannons.
english.ad_bf_110_c_fighter_equipment_1_desc: With the DB 601 engine widely available, the performance of the plane dramatically increased and nearly matched that the earlier models of the Bf 109 series. The Bf 110C was still armed with four MG17s and two 20mm MG FF cannons.
english.ad_bf_110_d_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Bf 110 D dramatically increased the range of the aircraft by adding a streamlined tank which was built under the fuselage, giving the plane a unique look and nickname Dacekbauch (dachshund’s belly). There were additional pair of fin-equipped drop tanks, one under each wing, that greatly increased the planes range at the cost of additional drag.\n\nObsolete BF110Cs can be converted to BF110Ds.
english.ad_bf_110_e_fighter_equipment_1_desc: : The Bf 110 E was designed as a fighter bomber, by adding racks under the wing enabling the plane to carry four 50kg bombs and a centerline rack carrying a 500kg bomb. The engine, armor and fuselage received upgrades; however, many pilots considered the aircraft slow, unresponsive, and one of the worst variants of the line.\n\nObsolete BF110Ds can be converted to BF110Es.
english.ad_bf_110_f_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Bf 110 F addressed the issues with the 110 Es by installing the new DB 601F engines, which produced nearly double the outpower of the planes original Jumo engines. Many pilots considered the Bf 110 F the best plane in the line, calling it aerobatic and smoother than the Bf 109, though not as fast.\n\nObsolete BF11ECs can be converted to BF110Fs.
english.ad_bf_110_g_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Bf 110 series was supposed to have been replaced by the Me 210; however, it was plagued with problems and further development of the Bf 110 occurred. The G series was fitted with more powerful DB 605B engines, upgraded nose armament which had two 30mm MK 108 cannons, and twin-barreled 7.92mm MG 81Zs. The G series were excellent night fighters and were armed with oft-bore gun system, which fired at an upward oblique angel and was devastating to enemy bombers, especially if the 37mm BK 3.7 auto fed cannon was installed.
english.ad_he_112_equipment_1_desc: : In 1933, the Reich Air Ministry finished a study which called for a fighter to have a top speed of 400 km/h at 6,000m and to be armed with a single 20mm MGC/30 or two 7.92mm MG 17s or one lightweight 20mm MG FF cannon with two MG 17s. The Heinkel He 112 designed by Walter and Siegfried Günter came in second place. The aircraft was heavier than its competitors but with an increased wing size the weight was more evenly distributed. The first production models featured two 7.92 MG17 and two 20mm MG FF cannons.
english.ad_he_112_equipment_2_desc: The main difference between a He 112 A and He 112 B was a more powerful engine, the Jumo 210Ga. The new engine increased performance, reduced fuel consumption, and ended up positively affecting the plane’s performance.
english.ad_fw_190_fighter_equipment_1_desc: When Kurt Tank’s design the Fw 159 lost the contest to have his plane become the backbone of the Luftwaffe, he vowed to create a better plane, which led to the Fw 190. The BMW 801 radial engine allowed the aircraft to carry larger loads than the Bf 109, which led to the Fw 190s success as a day fighter, fighter-bomber, ground-attack, and night fighter. The Fw 190 A was armed with six 7.92mm MG 17s and after the A-2 variant would have four MG17s and two 20mm MG 151/20E cannons.
english.ad_fw_190_fighter_equipment_2_desc: The Fw 190 A-5 was developed after tests determined the plane could easily carry additional ordinance. The plane easily carried a 250kg bomb and had wing-mounted racks for additional fuel tanks.\n\nObsolete FW 190 A-1s can be converted to FW 190 A-5s.
english.ad_fw_190_fighter_equipment_3_desc: The Fw 190 A-8 saw the more powerful BMW 801-D2 engines installed, additional armor, and an emergency boost system which raised the planes power for a few minutes. Later variants in the A-8 series replaced the 20mm cannons in the wings with 30mm MK 108 cannons.\n\nObsolete FW 190 A-5s can be converted to FW 190 A-8s.
english.ad_fw_190_interceptor_equipment_1_desc: : In order to address performance problems at high altitude, replacing turbocharged engines with supercharged engines and a pressurized cockpit were added. Two 30mm MK 108 cannons were installed in the wings to complement the two 20mm MG 151s. A later variant added an additional 30mm MK 108 cannon firing through the propeller hub.
english.ad_fw_190_f_equipment_1_desc: Following the success of the Fw 190 A-4, a true ground attack version was designed. Already having a centerline mounted bomb rack carrying a 250kg bomb, additional racks were installed under the wings carrying a total of four 50kg bombs.
english.ad_fw_190_g_equipment_1_desc: Following the success of the Fw 190 F, the G series was designed to extend the range of the aircraft. With the removal of two 20mm MG151 cannons and subsequent ammunition reduction, the Fw 190 G could carry a 500kg bomb on the centerline and two additional 250kg bombs, one on each wing.\n\nObsolete FW 190 Fs can be converted to FW 190 Gs.
english.ad_ta_152_fighter_equipment_1_desc: A Ta 152 variant armed with one 30mm cannon and four 20mm cannons, capable of both air-to-air and ground-attack missions.
english.ad_ta_152_fighter_equipment_2_desc: The Fw 190 was a good aircraft but suffered performance above 6,100 meters, the Ta 152 was further development of the Fw 190 aimed at increasing high-altitude performance. The fuselage was extended, the wings were greatly extended which increased high-altitude performance at the cost of speed at lower altitudes. A pressurized cockpit was added. The plane was armed with one 30mm MK 108 cannon and two 20mm MG151/20 cannons.
english.ad_bv_155_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The development of the Bv 155 began under Messerschmitt, which was designing a single-seat carrier-based fighter. In 1943, Blohm & Voss took over the design under the condition there was complete design freedom. Engineers determined there would need to be a complete redesign. The plane was re-envisioned as a high-altitude interceptor with a DB 603U engine with power turbosupercharger. The plane’s service ceiling was 16,950m. The armament went through various proposals, one or two 30mm MK 108 cannons with two 20mm MG151/20 cannons. The plane never saw combat action.
english.ad_he_100_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 100 was designed Ernst Heinkel as a new fighter that could leap beyond the performance seen in the Bf 109, which had greatly outperformed biplanes of the time. Working with Walter Günter, the He 100 was completely different than the He 112. The design included a number of drag reducing features, including having the landing gear fully enclosed in flight. The proposed armament was one 20mm MG FF cannon and two 7.92mm MG17s, one in each wing. The plane was rejected in order to concentrate on single-seat fighter development of the Bf 109 series.
english.ad_ar_197_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Arado Ar 197 was biplane designed for naval operations for the proposed aircraft carriers Graf Zeppelin and Peter Strasser. The third prototype of the plane was armed with two 7.92 MG17s and one 20mm MG FF, could carry four 50kg bombs and an auxiliary fuel tank. The plane never made it past the prototype stage because biplanes were hopelessly outclassed by newer designs like the BF 109 T and the Me 155.
english.ad_ar_234_scout_equipment_1_desc: The Arado Ar 234 B-1 was the reconnaissance version and was equipped with two Rb 50/30 or two Rb 75/30 cameras. The plane relied on its speed as it had no defensive weapons.
english.ad_ar_234_equipment_1_desc: The Arado Ar 234 was the world’s first operational jet-powered bomber with four engines. The payload included two 500kg bombs suspended from the engines or one 1,000kg under the fuselage with a max payload of 1,500kg. The plane did not have any defensive armaments and relied on its speed to avoid being intercepted. The Arado Ar 234 is the last Luftwaffe plane to fly over England during the war.
english.ad_ar_234_equipment_2_desc: The Arado Ar 234 C was equipped with lighter-weight BMW 003 engines that were mounted in a pair as twin-engine nacelles; which freed up 720kg of weight compared to the Jumo 004s, these engines were in high-demand for the Me 262. The new engines provided a better airspeed, a faster climb rate, and increased range.
english.ad_ar_65_equipment_1_desc: : The Arado Ar 65 was armed with two 7.92mm MG17s, had an increased wingspan and more powerful engine than previous Arado Ar designs. The aircraft was quickly relegated to a training role, with a dozen given to the Royal Bulgarian Air Force in 1937.
english.ad_ar_65_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Ar 65 F had improved flight performance over the Ar 65 E.
english.ad_ar_66_equipment_1_desc: The Ar 66 was a training aircraft also used for night harrasment.
english.ad_ar_68_equipment_1_desc: The Arado Ar 68 was a single seat biplane fighter, armed with two 7.92mm MG17 and capable of carrying 6 ten-kilogram fragmentation bombs. The design was intended to replace the Heinkel He 51. With a powerful Junkers Jumo 210 engine, the plane had an unforgiving high performance. The fighter saw action in the Spanish Civil War, where it was outclassed by the Soviet I-16. After being removed from frontline service, the plane was used as a training aircraft.
english.ad_ar_76_equipment_1_desc: The Arado Ar 76 was designed as a light fighter with a secondary role as an advanced trainer. The plane was armed with two 7.92mm MG17.
english.ad_ar_81_equipment_1_desc: Though the Junkers Ju 87 was already in the prototype stage, the Air Ministry had requested alternative designs. The Arado Ar 81 was an all-metal biplane, armed with a single 7.92mm MG17 in the front, a defensive 7.92mm MG15 in the rear, and capable of carrying 250kg of bombs. Though initially better at maneuverability, range, and rate of climb than the Junkers Ju 87, the Arado Ar 81 had less development potential due to its biplane design.
english.ad_ar_95_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Arado Ar 95 was designed as a single-engine reconnaissance and patrol biplane designed by Arado at the behest of Chile and Turkey. A variant of the Ar 95, the 195, was intended to serve as a torpedo bomber on the Graf Zeppelin. However, the design did not meet the specifications and the superior Fieseler Fi 167 was selected. At the start of the war, the Ar 95’s intended for Turkey were requisitioned by the Luftwaffe and used for training and coastal operations in the Baltic Sea.
english.ad_bv_138_equipment_1_desc: The Blohm & Voss Bv 138 was designed as a long-range maritime patrol and naval reconnaissance aircraft. The unique design and look of the plane earned it the nickname Der Fliegende Holzschuh (Flying Clog). The plane had two powered gun turrets, each with one 15mm MG151/20 autocannons and a 13mm MG 131 heavy machine gun behind the central engine. The payload consisted of six 50kg bombs or four 150kg depth charges.
english.ad_bv_238_equipment_1_desc: The Blohm & Voss Bv 238 was a gigantic flying boat weighing at 100 tons when fully loaded. The aircraft was powered by six DB 603 liquid-cooled engines. The plane carried a wide array of armaments, twenty 13mm MG131 and two 20mm MG151/20 autocannons. The payload included twenty 250kg bombs and four 1,000 kg bombs or an array of two 1,200 kg torpedoes, 4 Henschel Hs 293 missiles, or two 1,000kg BV 143 glide bombs. A crew of twelve was required to man the aircraft. A land variant, the Bv 250 was proposed as a transport, long-range bomber, and transatlantic reconnaissance duties.
english.ad_do_11_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Dornier Do 11 was initially considered a heavy bomber capable of carrying up to 1,000kg of bombs. The plane was notable for having only two engines and a retractable undercarriage, however the gears often did not work and left locked down. The airplane proved unpopular with pilots and after several attempted modifications and fixes, the Dornier Do 13 came into existence. The Do 13 suffered numerous crashes and never saw full production.
english.ad_do_wal_equipment_1_desc: The Dornier Do 16 J or Wal (Whale) was a twin-engine flying boat armed with three machine guns. The plane served as mail carrier, transport plane, and helped explore the Arctic regions. For military usage, the plane served for air-sea rescue and gunfire spotting for large ships.
english.ad_do_17_bomber_equipment_1_desc: Developed as a bomber fast enough to outrun enemy fighters, the Do 17 soon fell behind fighter aircraft development.
english.ad_do_17_bomber_equipment_2_desc: Attempting to address the shortcoming of the Dornier Do 17 E, the M variants were given a more powerful engines which improved performance. The bomb bay was reconfigured and now capable of holding up to 1,000kg of bombs.  A version of the plane existed using the DB601 engines, but since they were primarily used for fighter aircraft, only a few models were produced.\n\nObsolete Dornier Do 17 E’s can be converted to Dornier Do 17 M.
english.ad_do_17_scout_equipment_1_desc: The Dornier Do 17 started its life as a fast bomber but due to its lack of payload, short range, and slow speed it was discontinued from frontline service around 1940. With a need for reconnaissance vehicles, the P variant was created with more powerful BMW 132N radial engines, which increased performance, range, and reduced fuel consumption. The cameras of the craft were controlled remotely from the cockpit.\nObsolete Dornier Do 17 E and M’s can be converted to Dornier Do 17 P.
english.ad_do_17_z_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Dornier Do 17 Z series became the most recognizable plane of the Do 17s, the fuselage was redesigned with the cockpit being dropped, allowing a rear firing gunner position to be installed. The variant was originally tested with two DB 600 engines, however since they were reserved for single-seat fighters, the Bramo Fafnir 323 P engines were used. The planes bomb load was at first increased then decreased due to additional weight from upgraded features like new machine guns and another crew member. The days of the Do 17 as a bomber were numbered.\n\nObsolete Dornier Do 17 Ms can be converted to Dornier Do 17 Zs.
english.ad_do_17_night_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The success of the Dornier Do 17 Z as a bomber was short lived, however designs were made to fit new aircraft a solid nose from a Junker Ju 88, add a 20mm MG FF cannon and three 7.92mm MG17s and make the plane into a night fighter. The night fighter had three crew members, had better armor protection and was fitted with additional fuel tanks.
english.ad_do_18_equipment_1_desc: The Dornier Do 18 was a variant; a more developed Do 16 flying boat. It was powered by the new Junkers Jumo 205 diesel engines, which lowered fuel consumption. The airframe retained the distinct look of the Do 16 but was made more aerodynamically and hydrodynamically efficient. Beginning on March 27 and ending two days later, a Dornier Do 18 flew non-stop from Start Point Devon in the United Kingdom to Caravelas, Brazil, a distance of 8,391km. By the start of the war, the plane was obsolete and relegated to reconnaissance, training, and air and sea rescue in the North Sea and Baltic Sea.
english.ad_do_215_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Dornier Do 215 was originally designated as an export version of the Dornier Do 17Z, however a number served in the Luftwaffe in the role of light bomber, reconnaissance, and night fighter. The aircraft received new engines, the DB 601 Ba inline engines, which greatly increased the plane’s flight performance. The plane was produced in limited numbers.
english.ad_do_217_bomber_equipment_1_desc: Recognizing the need for a twin-engine bomber or long range reconnaissance plane, designers at Dornier went about creating a new plane, which became the Do 217. The plane featured two BMW 801A air-cooled engine, had a one-meter longer wingspan than the Do 17 and a bomb payload of up to 3,500kg. The plane could be fitted with a torpedo and three aerial mines instead of bombs. When it first entered operation, the plane was used for naval minelaying and anti-shipping operations in the North Sea.
english.ad_do_217_bomber_equipment_2_desc: The Dornier Do 217 received a new streamlined cockpit with a stepless design, which had first been used in the Heinkel He 111 P. The design eliminated the separate windscreen panels for the pilot, improving visibility. The new design made the aircraft more aerodynamic and the fastest design in the Do 217 series.\n\nObsolete Dornier Do 217 Es can be converted to Do 217 Ks.
english.ad_do_217_night_fighter_equipment_1_desc: Under increased attack by night-time attacks and with a shortage of the preferred Bf 110 Junker Ju 88Cs, a plan was made to modify existing Do 217s into night fighters. The J series was the first aircraft in the series and was fitted with a new solid nose, four 20mm MG FF cannons and four 7.92mm MG17s. The N series major of change of slanting the weapons at a 70-degree angle, this method was later known as Schraege Musik; which allowed planes to approach enemy bombers from underneath them. The J series also received the more powerful DB 603 A-1 engines. Due to its weight, the plane suffered reliability issues and was not very agile.
english.ad_do_217_gb_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Dornier Do 217 K-2 was a specialized anti-shipping variant and fitted with hardpoints that allowed the aircraft to carry two Fritz X guided bombs which were guided by the FuG 203 Kehl guidance system. The wings were greatly expanded by five meters which gave the K-2 a much better high-altitude performance.\n\nObsolete Dornier Do 217 E and Ks can be converted to Do 217 K-2s.
english.ad_do_22_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Dornier Do 22 was developed by Dornier’s Swiss subsidiary as a three-seat, single engine plane capable of carrying one 800kg torpedo or four 50kg bombs. Despite having good performance, the plane was constructed in small numbers and exported to Greece, Yugoslavia, and Finland.
english.ad_do_23_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Dornier Do 23 corrected many of the problems with the Dornier Do 11 and 13s. The plane could carry up to 1,000kg of bombs. By 1936, the aircraft was being replaced by the newer Dornier Do 17s and existing Do 23s were relegated to training duties. During the war a few Do 23s were used as minesweepers and fitted with current-carrying degaussing ring which used a magnetic field to trigger submerged naval mines.
english.ad_do_24_equipment_1_desc: The Dornier Do 24 was a three-engine flying boat designed for maritime patrol and search and rescue. The plane first saw use by the Royal Netherlands Navy in 1936 before being evaluated by the Luftwaffe against Blohm & Voss’s BV 138. Dornier stated the plane was accredited with rescuing over 12,000 people over its lifetime.
english.ad_do_317_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Dornier Do 317 was Dornier’s design for the “Bomber B” project, two versions existed; a simplified A variant or advanced B model. The B variant featured remotely aimed gun turrets, a higher bomb payload, extended wing, and a better powerplant. The airframe was designed with a pressurized cabin in mind, however trials revealed there was little performance gained over the Do 217s and the six prototypes were fitted with FuG 203 Kehl radio guidance transmitting gear and employed as Henschel Hs 293 anti-ship missile platforms.
english.ad_do_335_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Dornier Do 335 can trace its origins back to the first war when Claude Dornier had designed several flying boats using tandem engines. The use of tandem engines helped increase the planes roll rate, kept the planes weight on its centerline and reduced drag. The Dornier Do 335 was part of the Emergency Fighter Program directive and given maximum priority in production. The Dornier Do 335 A was armed with an engine mounted 30mm MK 103 cannon and two 20mm MG151/20s.
english.ad_do_335_fighter_equipment_2_desc: The Dornier Do 335 B saw several proposed variants, ranging from longer wings, two additional 30mm MK 103 cannons, extra fuel tanks and better engines. None of these variants left the design board.\n\nObsolete Dornier Do 335 As can be converted to Bs.
english.ad_fi_167_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Fieseler Fi 167 was designed as a carrier-based torpedo bomber that could also perform dive bombing. The plane had excellent handling capabilities, carried a large payload up to 1,000kg of bombs or a 765kg torpedo. Like the Fieseler Fi 156 Storch, the Fi 167 plane had great slow speed capabilities. Due to the Graf Zeppelin not scheduled to be completed till 1940, the production of the Fi 167 had low priority.
english.ad_fw_187_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Focke-Wulf Fw 187 Falke (Falcon) was designed by Kurt Tank as a twin-engine, high-performance fighter similar to the Bf 110. However, the Luftwaffe viewed it as an intermediate plane between the Bf 110 and its proposed successor the Me 210. The plane’s armament called for four 7.92mm MG17 and two 20mm MG FF cannons. Only nine prototypes were built.
english.ad_fw_189_scout_equipment_1_desc: The Focke Wulf 189 was designed as a three-seat reconnaissance plane with a good all-round view to support the ground forces and replace the Henschel Hs 126. The plane used two Argus As 410 engines, which were not in demand like the DB 600 and DB 601. The plane was relatively slow and looked fragile, however it had great maneuverability while turning and could outrun enemy fighters by flying in tight circles.
english.ad_fw_200_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Focke Wolf Fw 200 C series was designed as a naval bomber, capable of carrying a 1,000kg bomb or several naval mines. The additional fuel tanks, armor plating, defensive machine guns, and payload did not help the airframe.
english.ad_fw_200_bomber_equipment_2_desc: The Focke Wulf 200 C-3 featured structural improvements, two new 15mm MG 151 cannons, and a hardpoint for an additional 500kg bomb or extra fuel tank. The plane received new Bramo 323 R-2 radial engines. An additional feature was the inclusion of an improved Lotfe 7D bombsight, greatly improving the plane’s accuracy against ships.\n\nObsolete Focke Wulf 200 C-1s can be converted to Focke Wulf 200 C-3s.
english.ad_fw_200_c8_bomber_equipment_1_desc: : The Fw C-8 variant was fitted with the FuG 200 Hohentwiel low-UHF band search radar.  A few planes were fitted with the FuG 203b Kehl missile control transmitter, though the plane’s weak airframe and vulnerability to enemy aircraft did not make it an ideal naval bomber.\n\nObsolete Focke-Wulf 200 C-3s can be converted to Fw 200 C-8s.
english.ad_he_111_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 111 first masqueraded as a civil airliner, though from conception it was designed as a fast-medium bomber. The main internal bomb bay could carry 2,000kg of bombs and with external racks an additional 3,600kg could be carried, however it severely affected the plane’s performance. The plane could sustain heavy damage and remaining airborne. The plane would become the workhorse of the Luftwaffe, serving as a medium bomber, strategic bomber, torpedo bomber and transport plane. The Heinkel He 111 A served as the first prototype.
english.ad_he_111_bomber_equipment_2_desc: The first production version of the He 111 bomber.
english.ad_he_111_bomber_equipment_3_desc: The He 111 E had increased payload.
english.ad_he_111_bomber_equipment_4_desc: The He 111 F was built with upgraded engines and a modified wing.
english.ad_he_111_j_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The performance of the Heinkel He 111 at low-level flying interested the Kriegsmarine. Powered by the DB 600G engine, the plane could be armed with up to 2,000kg payload of torpedoes or naval mines. The more powerful engine was not widely available, leading to using older DB 600 models, which negatively affected the plane’s performance. Due to this and four-man crew, which the Kriegsmarine viewed as extravagant, the plane saw limited production.\n\nObsolete Heinkel He 111 A, B, E, and Fs can be converted to Heinkel He 111 Js.
english.ad_he_111_bomber_equipment_5_desc: The Heinkel He 111 P featured new liquid cooled DB 601A-1 engines and a newly designed nose section which allowed for the mounting of an additional 7.92mm MG15. The smooth glazed nose allowed pilots to have a better view. Additional features included an improved radio, self-sealing fuel tanks, and semi-retractable wheels to reduce drag.\n\nDue to major changes, obsolete Heinkel He 111 Fs cannot be converted to Heinkel He 111 Ps.
english.ad_he_111_h_bomber_equipment_1_desc: Due to delivery concerns of the liquid cooled DB 601 engines, the plane’s powerplant was switched to Junkers Jumo 211. The plane remained fairly like the He 111 P model, though some variants had cable-cutting equipment to counter barrage balloons. The Heinkel He 111 H series would be the most produced aircraft from Heinkel.\n\nObsolete Heinkel He 111 Ps can be converted to Heinkel He 111 Hs.
english.ad_he_111_h6_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 111 H-6 initiated overall improvements to the H series by installing Jumo 211 F-1 engines, which increased the planes speed. The climb rate was quicker and a slightly higher ceiling was achieved. The planes defensive armament was further increased with the addition of a 20mm MG FF cannon and additional 7.92mm MG15s.\n\nObsolete Heinkel He 111 Hs can be converted to Heinkel He 111 H-6s.
english.ad_he_111_h16_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 111 H-16 provided a great change in defensive armament as all 7.92mm MG15s were replaced with 13mm MG 131s in electrically powered turrets. The engines were upgraded to the Jumo 211 F-2s, improving speed and service ceiling. Radio equipment was installed in every aircraft, with some receiving FuG 200 Hohentwiel maritime radar. \n\nObsolete Heinkel He 111 H-6s can be converted to Heinkel He 111 H-16s.
english.ad_he_115_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 115 was a three-seat seaplane that was used as a torpedo bomber and performed duties such as reconnaissance and minelaying. The planes were well armed with two 7.92mm machine guns. Some variants had a 20mm cannon. The plane could carry up five 250kg bombs, two 250kg bombs and one 800kg torpedo or a 920kg sea mine. Norway ordered six Heinkel He 115s, which were delivered in 1939, four of which escaped to the United Kingdom when Norway was invaded.
english.ad_he_118_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 118, designed by the Günter brothers, was a competitor to the Junkers Ju 87. The plane was limited to bombing from a shallow angle of 50 degrees, unlike the Junkers Ju 87 at 90 degrees. In 1936, Ernst Udet took the Heinkel He 118 on a test flight and the plane’s propeller broke and the plane disintegrated. Heinkel was not awarded the contract.
english.ad_he_162_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 162 known as ‘Spat’ or Sparrow by Heinkel, Volksjäger (People’s Fighter) or Salamander, was a single-engine jet fighter constructed mostly of wood because of the shortage of strategic metals. The aircraft needed to be easy to fly, hopefully with only a short training regimen, preferably after flying a Deutsche Forschungsanstalt für Segelflug (German Institute for Glider Research) Stummel-Habicht. The plane ended up weighing 2,800kg, could travel between 790-905 km/h, and was armed with two 20mm MG151/20 cannons, though earlier variants had two 30mm MK 108 cannons. The realization of a people’s fighter was doomed because the aircraft required experienced pilots to handle properly.
english.ad_he_177_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 177 was designed as a long-range bomber under General Wever’s principal of being able to strike the Ural Mountains. In contrast to other long-range bombers, the He 177 was powered by two DB 606 engines capable of 2,000 horsepower each. These engines were new and suffered numerous teething pains such as catching on fire, earning the plane the nickname Reichsfeurzeug (Reich’s lighter). With an array of technical difficulties and multiple roles the He 177 entered service in 1942, though was still plagued with problems.
english.ad_he_177_bomber_equipment_2_desc: The A-3 series aimed to fix the problems with the A-1 and A-2s, which were plagued with engine problems. The fuselage was extended by 1.6 meters and the engines were relocated and replaced by DB 610 A/B engines. The electrical system was improved, and older defensive armament was replaced with newer equipment.\n\nDue to major changes, obsolete Heinkel He 177 A-1s cannot be converted to He 177 A-3s.
english.ad_he_177_bomber_equipment_3_desc: The A-5 was the main production series using the now standardized airframe from the A-3. The wings were strengthened to accommodate the installation of ETC 2000/XII wing racks. The defensive armament was further increased, replacing manned machine guns with remote controlled guns.\n\nObsolete Heinkel He 177 A-3s can be converted to He 177 A-5s.
english.ad_he_177_gb_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The A-5/R1 used the standardized airframe of the A-3 and A-5 series with minor optimizations for the installation of FX 1400 Fritz X and Hs 293 guided bombs, which were guided by FuG 203 Kehl radio guidance transmitting gear. The plane could carry three FX 1400 Fritz X or three Hs 293s.\n\nObsolete Heinkel He 177 A-5s can be converted into naval bombers.
english.ad_he_219_night_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 219 Uhu (Eagle-Owl) was a purpose built night fighter with a sophisticated design that included the Lichtenstein SN-2 VHF-band intercept radar, ejection seats, and tricycle landing gear. The aircraft was powered by the DB 603AA engines which allowed for high altitude flying. Two 30mm MK 108 cannons were installed in the Schraege Musik arrangement, allowing upward-firing against enemy bombers. Additional armament included four 20mm MG151/20 cannons, two in the wings and two under the fuselage. The development and production process was bitter due to political rivalries between Josef Hammhuber, commander of the night fighters, and Ernst Heinkel.
english.ad_he_45_equipment_1_desc: The He 45 C is an outdated reconnaissance bomber that can serve in night harrasment.
english.ad_he_46_scout_equipment_1_desc: A plane developed specifically for photo reconnaissance. Relies primarily on speed and stealth to survive and will generally lose in any stand-up fight.
english.ad_he_46_equipment_1_desc: A light reconnaissance bomber, the He 46 is outdated but can still serve in night harrasment.
english.ad_he_50_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 50 began life as a request by the Imperial Japanese Navy looking for a plane that matched the specifications of being a two-seat dive bomber, capable of carrying 250kg of bombs, launched from catapults, and capable of wheeled or float undercarriages. The plane was relegated to training schools until it was used in night harassment missions in the Eastern Front.
english.ad_he_51_equipment_1_desc: The He 51 is a biplane fighter aircraft.
english.ad_he_51_equipment_2_desc: The He 51 is a biplane fighter aircraft.
english.ad_he_51_equipment_3_desc: Originally designed as a biplane fighter, the Heinkel He 51 struggled as a fighter, being outclassed by Soviet aircraft. It found success in the ground-attack role and helped develop close support tactics. After 1938, the plane was delegated as an advanced trainer.
english.ad_he_66_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 50 began life as a request by the Imperial Japanese Navy who were interested in a plane that would be a two-seat dive bomber, could carry 250kg of bombs, launched from catapults and capable of wheeled or float undercarriages. The third prototype, HE-50B was re-designated as the HE-66 and sent to Japan. It would become the basis for the Aichi-D1A.
english.ad_he_70_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 70 was originally designed as a mail and faster passenger aircraft, though its career as a commercial plane was short lived. The plane racked up a total of eight world speed records in 1933. The military took interest in the plane and converted it to a fast bomber capable of carrying six 50kg or twenty-four 10kg of bombs. The plane saw service in the Spanish Civil War as a reconnaissance plane where it was nicknamed “Rayo” or “Lightning”.\n\nObsolete Heinkel He 70 E’s can be converted into Heinkel He 70 F Recon planes.
english.ad_he_70_scout_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 70 was originally designed as a mail and faster passenger aircraft, though its career as a commercial plane was short lived. The plane initially served as a bomber, though its payload was minimal and during the Spanish Civil War the plane was used for reconnaissance. Due the plane’s speed, it was great for these types of missions and had little defense to protect itself from enemy aircraft.\nObsolete Heinkel He 70 E Fast Bombers can be converted into Heinkel He 70 F Recon planes.
english.ad_hs_123_equipment_1_desc: One of the first aircraft designed by Henschel, a locomotive manufacturer, the Henschel Hs 123 was a single-seat biplane dive bomber and close support attack aircraft. Armed with two 7.92mm MG17 and capable of carrying up to 450kg of bombs, the plane failed in its role as a dive bomber but proved successful during the Spanish Civil War in the ground attack role. The planes were nicknamed “Angelito” (dear angel or little angel) by the Spanish. The plane would remain in combat roles until 1944.
english.ad_hs_126_equipment_1_desc: The Hs 126 was a reconnaissance aircraft also used for night harrasment.
english.ad_hs_126_scout_equipment_1_desc: The Henschel Hs 126 was a two-seat reconnaissance and observation aircraft derived from the Henschel Hs 122. The plane received praise for its short takeoff and low speed, which were beneficial at the time. The plane served as a short-range recon and observer before being replaced by general purpose craft like the Fieseler Fi 156 Storch and medium-range Focke-Wulf Fw 189 Uhu.
english.ad_hs_129_equipment_1_desc: The Henschel Hs 129 was designed with one primary restraint, it could use other engines in demand, like the DB 600 and DB 601. First the aircraft used the Argus As 410, which left the plane severely underpowered and barely able to fly. The B1 redesign used the French Gnome-Rhône 14M, which made the aircraft perform exceptionally well. Originally armed with two 7.92mm MG17 guns, and two 20mm MG 151/20 cannons, planes were later armed with a 30mm MK 101 cannon with armor-piercing ammunition.
english.ad_hs_129_equipment_2_desc: One of the primary differences between the B1 series and B2 series was the upgraded cannon pack which replaced the 30mm MK 101 cannon with 30mm MK 103, which fired at twice the rate. Field reports soon indicated the weapon was ineffective against newer Soviet tanks and a field pack was distributed installing a 37mm BK anti-tank cannon, like the weapons installed on the Junkers Ju 87G. Only a few B2s were produced before the B3 line, which carried a 75mm Rheinmetall Pak 40, entered service.\n\nObsolete Hs 129 B1s can be converted to Hs 129 B2s.
english.ad_hs_132_cas_equipment_1_desc: The Henschel Hs 132 featured an unorthodox design with the BMW 003 jet engine mounted on the top of the fuselage and the pilot laying in the prone position, which would reduce the effect of g-forces. The Hs 132C replaced the BMW engine with a larger Heinkel HeS 011, added two 20mm MG151/20 cannons and two 30mm MK 103 cannons, in addition to the one 500kg bomb payload.
english.ad_ju_188_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Ju 188 was designed to fit the criteria of the “Bomber B” program to create a second-generation bomber capable of high speed, long range and higher payload. The aircraft utilized BMW 801 G-2 engines and carried up to 3,000kg of bombs. Plans existed to create different variants, a night fighter, reconnaissance, and a high-altitude bomber. The high-altitude model featured a pressurized cabin; however, the bomb payload was greatly reduced.
english.ad_ju_188_nav_bomber_equipment_1_desc: TThe Junkers Ju 188 E featured a low-UHF-band FuG 200 Hohentwiel sea-search radar and the outer wing bomb racks were removed to make room for a torpedo. The increased payload of bombs and torpedoes reduced the performance of the aircraft.\n Obsolete Junker Ju 188 As can be converted to Ju 188 Es.
english.ad_ju_288_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Junker Ju 288 originally started as a project headed by an engineer at Heinkel, but when he left for Junkers, the design went with him. The Ju 288 was the winner of the “Bomber B” project, a successor to the fast bombers currently in operation. The aircraft was designed with Jumo 222 engines with 1,500 kW output, however the engines suffered immense teething pains and eventually dropped for less powerful powerplants. The plane never went into production status though two prototypes were fitted with defensive armament and deployed to the Western Front.
english.ad_ju_290_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Junkers Ju 290 was derived from the four-engine Ju 90 civilian airliner which could carry up to 40 passengers. The plane was intended to replace the cumbersome Focke-Wulf Fw 200 Condor, which had proven to be vulnerable to enemy aircraft and had a weak airframe. The Ju 290 was slow to roll off the production lines due to defensive modifications. The aircraft carried the FuG 200 Hohentwiel low-UHF band search radar and could locate enemy convoys from up to 80 km away. The Ju 290 was looked at being a long-range transport to Japan, though never undertook such a mission. A special variant was created for Hitler, his compartment having 12mm armor plating, 50mm bullet proof glass, and a special escape hatch with a parachute built into the seat.
english.ad_ju_290_gb_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Junkers Ju 290 A-7 was fitted with the FuG 203 Kehl radio guidance system and could carry either three Fritz Xs or three Henschel Hs 293 radio-guided missiles.\n\nObsolete Junker Ju 290s can be converted to radio guided bombers.
english.ad_ju_388_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Reich Aviation Ministry learned about the American B-29 in late 1942. The plane’s rumored altitude put it outside of the range of the Luftwaffe’s existing anti-aircraft guns and only the rare 128mm FlaK 40 could fire up to 14,800 meters. The Junkers 88 had served as a versatile plane and additional design work led to the Ju 188, and eventually the Ju 388. The Junkers Ju 388 was designed to serve as a heavy bomber and night fighter, torpedo bomber, photoreconnaissance, and high-altitude bomber. The Ju 388 K could carry up to 3,000 kg of bombs.
english.ad_ju_488_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Junkers Ju 488 was conceived as a stopgap long-range bomber using a mismatch of existing designs. The airframe was based on the Ju 188, the tail from the Ju 288. The wings were extended an additional mid-section was added to the fuselage, which allowed for the addition of two engines, bring the total to four. The defensive armament featured two 20mm MG151 cannons in remote tail turrets. Aircraft production was subcontracted out to French companies and the first prototype was destroyed by the French resistance in July 1944.
english.ad_ju_52_bomber_equipment_1_desc: While originally designed as a transport aircraft, bomber versions of the Ju 52 were pressed into service due to the unexpected hole left by the problematic Do 11/13/23 program.
english.ad_ju_86_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Junkers Ju 86 began life as twin-engine high-speed civilian airliner, capable of carrying ten passengers, and a medium bomber. The plane originally had Jumo 205 diesel engines, which when used in combat during the Spanish Civil War, proved unreliable. The Junkers Ju 86 D had two Siemens SAM 22, which along with an improved tail, increased the performance and stability of the plane. The plane proved inferior to the Heinkel He 111.
english.ad_ju_86_bomber_equipment_2_desc: Designed as an export craft, the Junkers Ju 86 E had BMW 132 engine, which further increased the reliability of the plane. The aircraft proved of little military use and saw more life as a civil airliner for several countries including Sweden, Bolivia, South Africa, Switzerland, Chile, and Australia.
english.ad_ju_86_p_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Junker Ju 86 P was redesigned with a longer wingspan, a pressurized cabin, a new Junkers Jumo 207A-1 turbocharged engine and a two-man crew. The plane could reach an altitude of 12,000 meters. Due to its high altitude, the plane thrived in the long-range photo reconnaissance and high-altitude bombing. However, the effectiveness of the plane’s high-altitude was countered by British Westland Welkins, modified Supermarine Spitfire V’s and Soviet Yakovlev Yak-9PDs.\n\nObsolete Junker Ju 86 E and Ds can be converted to Junker Ju 86 Ps.
english.ad_ju_86_scout_equipment_1_desc: Though ineffective as a bomber, the Junker Ju 86 soon received a longer wingspan, a pressurized cabin, a new Junkers Jumo 207A-1 turbocharged engine and a two-man crew. The plane could reach an altitude of 12,000 meters. Due to its high altitude, the plane thrived in the long-range photo reconnaissance. The later series, the Ju 86 R used even larger wings and a more powerful engine reaching a ceiling of 16,000 meters.\n\nObsolete Junker Ju 86s can be converted to Junker Ju 86 Rs.
english.ad_ju_87_equipment_1_desc: The Junkers Ju 87 was designed by Hermann Pohlmann with one principle in mind, a dive bomber needed to be simple and robust. Following this principle, many technical innovations like discarding the retractable undercarriage for the fixed landing gear were implemented. Initial prototypes were powered by a Rolls-Royce Kestrel engine before being replaced with a German DB 600. The Junkers Ju 87 overcame competition from the Heinkel He 118, because Ernst Udet crashed on July 27th, 1936.
english.ad_ju_87_equipment_2_desc: The primary differences between a Junkers Ju 87 A and B was that the latter could now carry a two-person crew. The plane’s airframe was subdivided into sections to allow for transport by rail or truck. The plane retained two 7.92mm MG17s, one in each wing, and one 7.92mm MG15 in the rear for defensive purposes. The bomb load was either one 250kg or four 50kg bombs.\nObsolete Ju 87As can be converted to Ju 87Bs.
english.ad_ju_87_cv_equipment_1_desc: The Junkers Ju 87 C was intended to be a dive and torpedo bomber for the Kriegsmarine. The Ju 87 C had special equipment like a two-seat rubber dinghy with a flare gun, quick fuel dump mechanism and two inflatable bags under each wing and another two in the fuselage which would allow the plane to remain afloat on calm seas for three days. With the war under way in 1939, the order for 120 Junker Ju 87 Cs was cancelled, though tests of the plane continued.\nObsolete Junker Ju 87 A, B, and B-2’s can be converted to Junker Ju 87 C.
english.ad_ju_87_equipment_3_desc: The Ju 87 B-2 series included the more powerful Jumo 211D engine, a completely redesigned fuselage, landing gear, and lighter-weight wheel spats. The famous sirens were installed in the B-1 and B-2 series; however, they caused a loss of between 20-25 km/h and were eventually removed or replaced with whistles on the fin. The B-2 included further improvements like ski-equipped and a tropical kit.\n\nObsolete Ju 87Bs can be converted to Ju 87B-2s.
english.ad_ju_87_equipment_4_desc: The Ju 87 D series was an attempt to correct the vulnerabilities exposed in the early stages of the war. Armor protection of the plane was increased, along with the installation of a dual-barrel 7.92mm MG 81Z in the rear. A new more powerful engine, the Jumo 211J was installed, allowing the aircraft to carry up to 1,800kg of bombs. In addition, fuel capacity was increased, and the option to install drop tanks to the wings could allow a flight time of four hours.\n\nDue to major changes, obsolete Ju 87 B-2s cannot be converted to Ju 87 Ds.
english.ad_ju_87_cv_equipment_2_desc: he Ju 87 D-4 variant was a proposed torpedo bomber which would operate aboard the Graf Zeppelin. The aircraft was to carry a 750-950kg aerial torpedo based off the Japanese Type 91 design, which was specifically for ships in shallow water. Unlike other D series variants, the D-4  had two 20mm MG151/20 cannons, and the rear gunner’s ammunition was increased to 2,000 rounds.\nObsolete Junker Ju 87 Ds can be converted to Junker Ju 87 D-4s.
english.ad_ju_87_equipment_5_desc: The Ju 87 D-3 featured a slightly larger wing span than previous variants and the two 7.92mm MG17s were replaced with 20mm MG151/20s, better fitting the planes ground-attack role. The window in the cockpit’s floor was reinforced.\n\nObsolete Junker Ju 87Ds can be converted to Ju 87D-5s.
english.ad_ju_87_cv_equipment_3_desc: The Junkers Ju 87 E was a design for an improved carrier-capable version of the Stuka. The E series feature additional armor, wing cannons, and extended wing panels.\n\nObsolete Junker Ju 87 Ds can be converted to Junker Ju 87 Es.
english.ad_ju_87_cv_equipment_4_desc: The Ju 87 E was a design for an improved carrier-capable version of the Stuka, capable of both dive bombing and torpedo bombing. It never left the drawing board. This is the torpedo bombing version.
english.ad_ju_88_bomber_equipment_1_desc: Originally designed as a three-seat, high-speed bomber with a payload up to 800kg, the Junker Ju 88 was radically modified before entering production, the plane changed from being a bomber to a heavy dive bomber. The wings of the plane were strengthened, dive breaks were added, the fuselage was extended, and the number of crew increased from three to four. The first production models had a cable-cutting equipment to counter barrage balloons. The plane was armed with several defensive machine guns and could carry up to 1,000kg of bombs.
english.ad_ju_88_a4_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Junker Ju 88 A-4 set out to fix many of the issues that plagued the A-1. The plane received a longer wingspan and redesigned wingtips, new Jumo 211 J-1 engines, better propellers, and a reinforced undercarriage. Hardpoints were installed for four external bomb racks.\n\nDue to major changes, obsolete Junker Ju 88 A-1s cannot be converted to Ju 88 A-4s.
english.ad_ju_88_c6b_night_fighter_equipment_1_d: The Ju 88 C-6b was a night fighter derived from the Ju 88 bombers.
english.ad_ju_88_d_scout_equipment_1_desc: The need a long range and high-altitude photoreconnaissance was necessary. The Ju 88 D used A-4 fuselages, with empty bomb bays. The only difference was the use of metal propellers instead of wooden propellers.\n\nObsolete Ju 88 A-4s can be converted to Ju 88 Ds.
english.ad_ju_88_a17_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Junkers Ju 88 A-17 replaced the two bomb racks under each wing with one torpedo rack.\nObsolete Junker Ju 88 As can be converted to Ju 88 A-17s
english.ad_ju_88_s_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Junkers Ju 88 S was a high speed bomber with a smoothly glazed nose which increased the aerodynamic performance of the aircraft. A GM-1 nitrous-oxide boost system was installed, which increased the amount of oxygen in the fuel mixture and led to better high-altitude performance. Additional S series variants would add better powerplants and increase the bomb payload by using wooden bomb bay extensions.\n\nDue to major changes, previous Ju 88s cannot be converted to Ju 88 Ss.
english.ad_ju_88_p_equipment_1_desc: The Junkers Ju 88 P was an anti-tank and bomber destroyer variant with a different a 75mm, 50mm or twin 37mm caliber of cannon in a conformal ventral fuselage gun mount. The tank was produced in a small series and were perceived as a failure in both anti-tank and anti-bomber use. The P-1 variant featured a single 75mm cannon. P-2 and P-3 had two 37mm cannons, though P-3 featured more armor. The P-4 variant had a single 50mm cannon. A proposed P-5 variant would have been armed with a single 88mm cannon.\n Obsolete Junker Ju 88 As can be converted to Ju 88 Ps.
english.ad_ju_88_t_scout_equipment_1_desc: The Junkers Ju 88 T was based on the Ju 88S series, and featured a smooth glazed nose and an added GM-1 nitrous-oxide boost to increase the speed. The T series was a three-seat photoreconnaissance version, and the bomb bays were fitted with extra fuel and GM-1 nitrous-oxide tanks.\n\nDue to major changes, obsolete Ju 88s cannot be converted Ju 88 Ts.
english.ad_ju_89_bomber_equipment_1_desc: Beginning in 1933, General Walther Wever realized the importance of strategic bombing would play in the any upcoming war. Wever began talks with Dornier and Junkers in creating a long-range bomber. The proposed armament of the plane had two 20mm MG FF cannons, two 7.92mm MG 15s, and a payload of 1,600kg. Initial prototypes of the Junkers Ju 89 proved promising, however with General Wever’s death in 1936, his successors at the Luftwaffe favored dive bombers and close ground support.
english.ad_me_155_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Messerschmitt Me 155 was designed as a carrier-based single-seat fighter. To aid in the construction of the aircraft, the design incorporated as many components as possible from the Bf 109 G, but featured an entirely new wing, the undercarriage retracted inwards. The armament was to be an engine mounted 20mm MG151 cannon, two 20mm MG151 cannons and two 13mm MG131s, one in each wing. The delay in the construction of the Graf Zeppelin caused Messerschmitt to shelve their design, which was eventually picked up by Blohm & Voss.
english.ad_me_163_equipment_1_desc: The Messerschmitt Me 163 began as a design started in 1937 under the Deutsche Forschungsanstalt für Segelflug (German Institute for Glider Research). Due to design and prototype production differences, Alexander Lippisch left to work with Messerschmitt. The delay caused by this transition was beneficial as it allowed rocket engine technology to catch up. In prototype testing the Me 163 V4 set a world speed record at 1,004.5km/h. The plane went through numerous refinements before the B-series entered production, armed with two 30mm MK 108 cannons, which were accurate only at short range. The aircraft’s immense speed, short weapon range, climb rate and low fuel made combat time about five minutes.
english.ad_me_163_equipment_2_desc: The Messerschmitt Me 163 C featured a larger wing, an extended fuselage with extra capacity for fuel, and a pressurized cockpit with a bubble canopy which improved visibility. The maximum altitude increased to 15,850 meters and combat time increased to about nine minutes. There were plans to add a Sondergerät SG 500 Jagdfaust, a 50mm anti-bomber recoilless rifle, pointing upwards in the Schraege Musik method.
english.ad_me_210_fighter_equipment_1_desc: Design work on the Me 210, the successor to the Bf 110, began before the latter’s production version even took flight. Though using many of the same design concepts, the Me 210 had a shorter nose area, an internal bomb bay, and wings designed for higher cruise speeds. Powered by DB 601F engines, the plane could fly nearly as fast as some single-engine fighters. However, there were a series of design flaws that prevented the Me 210 from seeing service until 1943.
english.ad_me_262_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Messerschmitt Me 262 Schwalbe (Swallow) was the world’s first operational jet powered aircraft. Design work began before the start of the war, but problems with metals, engines, and political interference kept the plane from seeing operational status until mid-1944. The Me 262 was powered by a Jumo 004B, which used a minimal amount of strategic materials and was simpler to manufacture. The operational lifespan of the Jumo 004B, requiring an overhaul after 25 hours, would be used for another 10 hours before needing a new turbine wheel. The Me 262 jet fighter was armed with six nose mounted guns, two 20mm MG151/20 cannons, two 30mm MK 103 cannons, and two 30mm MK 108 cannons.
english.ad_me_262_cas_equipment_1_desc: TThe Messerschmitt Me 262 Schwalbe (Swallow) was the world’s first operational jet powered aircraft. Design work began before the start of the war, but problems with metals, engines, and political interference kept the plane from seeing operational status until mid-1944. The Me 262 was powered by a Jumo 004B, which used a minimal amount of strategic materials and was simpler to manufacture. The operational lifespan of the Jumo 004B, requiring an overhaul after 25 hours, would be used for another 10 hours before needing a new turbine wheel. The Me 262 jet fighter was armed with six nose mounted guns, two 20mm MG151/20 cannons, two 30mm MK 103 cannons, and two 30mm MK 108 cannons.
english.ad_me_264_bomber_equipment_1_desc: : The Messerschmitt Me 264 origins begin as a long-range reconnaissance aircraft project before being modified into a heavy bomber. The Me 264 was designed as an all-metal four-engine bomber and the fuselage was very lightly armored and carried few defensive armaments, the idea was to increase fuel capacity and range. Interest in the aircraft dwindled and the project was cancelled in September 1944. Messerschmitt then proposed a six-engine version the Me 264/6m or Me 364, but it never left the drawing board.
english.ad_me_410_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Me 410 was further development of the failed Me 210. With a different wing configuration, a longer fuselage and more powerful engines, the plane was renamed. The aircraft was armed with two 7.92mm MG 17s, two 20mm MG151/20 cannons, and two defensive 13mm MG131s. Four 21cm Werfer-Granate 21 rockets could be attached and up to 1,000kg in bombs. The Me 410 was Hitler’s favorite bomber destroyer but ended up serving mostly in reconnaissance roles after mid-1944
english.ad_ta_154_night_fighter_equipment_1_desc: Originally planned as a fast attack-bomber designated the Ta 211, the plane would be constructed primarily out of plywood bonded by a special phenolic resin adhesive – similar to the British DH.98 Mosquito. The only metal was used in a pressurized cockpit. The plane was powered by the Jumo 213 engines and armed with two 20mm MG151/20 cannons and two 30mm MK 108 cannons. Later variants were planned to have two fuselage-mounted 30mm MK 108 cannons in the Schraege Musik method. The plane suffered reliability issues because the plywood and adhesive caused chemical corrosion and the plywood suffered delamination.
english.ad_ta_254_night_fighter_equipment_1_desc: The Ta 254 was proposed further development of the Ta 154. The aircraft was designed with retractable tricycle landing gear, would have two engines either being DB 603E, DB 603Ls or Jumo 213Es. When compared to the Ta 154, the 254’s wings would have been longer. There would be several proposed variants as a day and night fighter, with the latter being armed with two fuselage-mounted 30mm MK 108s emplying Schraege Musik method, two forward-facing 20mm MG151 cannons and two forward-facing 30mm MK 108 cannons. The aircraft never left the drawing board.\n\nDue to major changes, obsolete Ta 154s cannot be converted to Ta 254s.
english.ad_he_59_bomber_equipment_1_desc: The Heinkel He 59 was concealed as a civil aircraft, though served as a torpedo bomber and reconnaissance plane able to operate on wheeled landing gear or twin-floats. The plane had an armament of three 7.92mm MG15s and could carry two 500kg, four 250kg, twenty 50kg or one 800kg torpedo. The plane served as a torpedo bomber during the early stages of the war before serving as a trainer craft.
english.ad_boeing_p12_equipment_1_desc: Fighters are aircraft designed to attack and destroy enemy aircraft.
english.ad_boeing_p12_equipment_2_desc: Fighters are aircraft designed to attack and destroy enemy aircraft.
english.ad_usa_boeing_p26_equipment_2_desc: Unit Type: Fighter\n\nThe Boeing P-26 was the first all metal production fighter aircraft and pursuit monoplane. The plane was powered by Pratt & Whitney R-1340-33 engines and had a high landing speed, which proved difficult for many pilots. Due to its diminutive size, the plane was affectionately known as the Peashooter. Armament included two .30 M1919 Browning machine guns or one .30 M1919 and one .50 caliber machine gun. Payload included two 100 pound or five 31-pound anti-personal bombs.
english.ad_curtiss_p36_equipment_1_desc: Unit Type: Fighter \n\n The Curtiss P-36 Hawk featured a sleek all-metal monoplane design and was powered by a Pratt & Whitney R-1830-17 Twin Wasp radial engine with 1,050 horsepower. Offensive armament included one .30 M1919 Browning machine gun and one .50 M2 machine gun. A hardpoint was added for a bomb rack which could carry a single 100-pound bomb. The plane is better known as the Curtis Hawk 75, an export model which saw service in numerous countries during the 1930s and 1940s.
english.ad_brewster_b239_equipment_1_desc: Fighter aircraft are used to destroy enemy aircraft using their high speed and manoeuvrability. Their light weapons will encounter difficulty against large bombers.
english.ad_curtiss_p40_equipment_1_desc: Unit Type: Fighter \n\n The Curtiss P-40B Warhawk was a single-engine, all-metal fighter and ground-attack vehicle that was a modification of the P-36 Hawk. The plane was very agile and low and medium altitudes but suffered from the lack of a supercharger which affected its performance at high altitudes. The semi-modular design of the aircraft made it easy to maintain even in the harshest of climates and conditions. The structure was well designed with a five-spar wing support, which allowed the plane to pull high-G turns. The early armament of two .30 M1919 Browning machine guns and two .50 M2 machine guns was described as inadequate.
english.ad_curtiss_p40_equipment_2_desc:
Unit Type: Fighter 

 The Curtis P-40E Warhawk featured a better engine and the installation of bomb racks under the wings, allowing a total of 2,000-pounds of bombs. The armament was upgraded to a total of six .50 M2 Browning machine guns, three in each wing. The plane was supplied to Commonwealth nations and was known as the Kittyhawk Mk IA.

Obsolete Curtiss P-40Bs can be converted to P-40Es.
english.ad_curtiss_p40f_equipment_1_desc:
Unit Type: Fighter 

 The Curtis P-40F Warhawk featured a new engine, the Packard V-1650 Merlin which increased the plane’s performance at high altitudes. The plane was supplied to Commonwealth nations and was known as the Kittyhawk Mk II.

Obsolete Curtiss P-40Es can be converted to P-40Fs.
english.ad_northamerican_mustang_equipment_1_des: Unit Type: Fighter \n\n The P-51 was a long-range, single-seat fighter and fighter-bomber designed by the North American Aviation company, which had been approached to build Curtiss P-40 Warhawks, under license. Instead, North American designed a new modern fighter, originally powered by an Allison V-1710 engine, which hampered the plane’s performance at high-altitudes. The P-51 first saw combat with the Royal Air Force as part of lend-lease.
english.ad_northamerican_p51b_equipment_1_desc:
Unit Type: Fighter 

 The P-51B was an improvement of the earlier version and replaced the Allison V-1710 with the Rolls-Royce Merlin, which greatly increased the aircraft’s performance at high-altitudes.

Obsolete P-51s can be converted to P-51Bs.
english.ad_northamerican_p51d_equipment_1_desc:
Unit Type: Fighter 

 The P-51D increased the armament of the plane to include six 0.50 M2 Browning machine guns and added hardpoints to carry one 500-pound bomb. Later variants in the P-51D series included six to ten 5-inch T64 High Velocity Aircraft Rockets.

Obsolete P-51Bs can be converted to P-51Ds.
english.ad_northamerican_p51h_equipment_1_desc:
Unit Type: Fighter 

 The P-51H shared little in common with previous variants, having received a smaller landing gear, a modified fuselage that was thinner but longer. The wheels received new disc brakes and a newer lightweight propeller was installed. Fuel amount was increased along with ammunition. A variant of the P-51H modified for use by the Navy. The plane received folded wings, an arrester hook, and additional external fuel tanks.

Due to significant changes, obsolete P-51s CANNOT be converted to P-51Hs.
english.ad_curtiss_p1_equipment_1_desc: While becoming increasingly obsolete, these aircraft are often the only ones available to smaller countries.
english.ad_curtiss_p1_equipment_2_desc: While becoming increasingly obsolete, these aircraft are often the only ones available to smaller countries.

english.ad_usa_boeing_p26_equipment_1_desc: Unit Type: Interceptor\n\nThe Boeing P-26 was the first all metal production fighter aircraft and pursuit monoplane. The plane was powered by Pratt & Whitney R-1340-33 engines and had a high landing speed, which proved difficult for many pilots. Due to its diminutive size, the plane was affectionately known as the Peashooter. Armament included two .30 M1919 Browning machine guns or one .30 M1919 and one .50 caliber machine gun.
english.ad_seversky_p35_equipment_1_desc: Unit Type: Interceptor \n\n The Seversky P-35 was an the first single-seat fighter in for the Army Air Corps to feature an all-metal construction, had retractable landing gear, and an enclosed cockpit. In order to help save weight, the wings were designed as wet wings, where the wings are sealed and used as fuel tanks. The plane was armed with two .30 M1919 Browning machine guns and two .50 M2 machine guns. Though the plane was quite rugged, it suffered poor performance and fuel was known to leak from the wings.
english.ad_republic_p43_equipment_1_desc: Unit Type: Interceptor \n\n The Republic P-43 Lancer was a single-engine, all-metal, low-wing monoplane fighter aircraft with very good performance at high altitudes and featured an effective oxygen system for the pilot. The aircraft was exceptional at long range flights, rivaled only by the Lockheed P-38 Lightning. Due to its high speed and high-altitude capabilities, the P-43 was employed in photo reconnaissance missions. The plane was well-armed with four .50 M2 Browning machine guns.
english.ad_bell_p39_equipment_2_desc: Unit Type: Interceptor \n\n Further development of Bell’s P-39 Airacobra. The N variant was designed with a longer propeller and reduced fuel tank and maintained an armament of one 37mm M4 cannon, two .50 M2 Browning machine guns which were nose-mounted, and one .50 M2 in each wing. The plane was sent to the Soviet Union by lend-lease, where it had a good combat record.
english.ad_bell_p63_equipment_1_desc: Unit Type: Interceptor \n\n The P-63 Kingcobra was the successor to the P-39, it incorporated suggestions and complaints from pilots. The wings were redesigned and carried more fuel, and a new engine was added with an efficient turbo-supercharger, improving the planes performance at high-altitudes. The 37mm M4 was replaced with a newer M10 37mm cannon with more rounds and a higher rate of fire. The aircraft also had two .50 M2 Browning machine guns which were nose-mounted, and one .50 M2 in each wing. The design was rejected by the Army Air Forces but was widely used by the Soviet Union.
english.ad_republic_p47m_equipment_1_desc: Unit Type: Interceptor \n\n With the appearance of advanced technology by the enemy, Republic developed a high-speed variant of the P-47. The engine was replaced with a 2,800 horsepower R-2800-57C with a powerful supercharger, dive brakes, and an improved propeller. Overall, the plane’s top speed increased to 473 mph. The aircraft maintained the same armament as other models, eight .52 M2 Browning machine guns, four in each wing.
english.ad_boeing_256_equipment_1_desc: Multi-role aircraft are designed to fufill both the functions of fighters in attacking enemy aircraft, as well as CAS in attacking enemy ground troops and ships.
